Maynooth University research page (water+salt, heat and cool; no fuel, prepared start state or continuous power; reuse up to 25 in a row; correct after 15 months). EurekAlert 16 Sep 2026 and SciTechDaily 13 Oct 2026 (10+3 in 30 s; numbers about 11-34 million in up to 14 h; not as fast as silicon). 'World first' wording appears only in press copy and is not used. Not stored or shown.
title: A tube of DNA, water and salt that works out sums
description: A computer made of DNA. One long DNA strand floats in salty water with many short DNA pieces that compete to stick along it. When the mix is heated and then cooled, the pieces settle into the most stable pattern they can, and that pattern spells out the answer. Nothing has to keep powering it while it works.
capability: Scientists can now make a tube of DNA, water and salt work out sums like addition and multiplication just by heating it and letting it cool, with no electricity running while it computes. It is still a lab experiment, far slower than a computer chip.
useCases: Doing simple math in a test tube of DNA, like adding two numbers or multiplying by 3, without plugging anything in while it works.
Reusing the same tube for up to 25 calculations in a row, or keeping it for over a year and still getting right answers.
body:
In September 2026, researchers reported a computer built from DNA instead of a chip. They mix a long DNA strand and many short DNA pieces with water and salt, heat it, and let it cool. As it cools, the short pieces compete for places along the long strand, and the most stable pattern they end up in is the answer. It needs no fuel, no special starting setup and no power running while it works. They ran 10 different programs and more than 700 calculations, including adding, multiplying by 3, dividing by 2, and checking whether a string of ones and zeros has an odd or even number of ones.

A small sum like 10 plus 3 took under a minute. The biggest job, adding two numbers as large as about 33 million, took up to 14 hours. The same mix worked for up to 25 calculations in a row, and one setup still gave correct answers after 15 months. But it is a lab experiment, not a product, and it is much slower than a computer chip. Bigger problems need slower cooling. The team hopes ideas like this could one day help store data in DNA or work inside living cells, but neither has been shown yet.
